notes: v1 drew it at ~1.90 m2 but that figure is a Homestyler area of a freehand polygon, NOT a requirement. The immovable V2 shaft stands in this corner; the recorded precedent is to build the cupboard AGAINST the obstruction rather than around it.

statement: A storage block containing TWO wardrobes that face OPPOSITE ways - one opening onto the hall, the other onto the kids' room.
anchored_to: between the hall and the kids' room
notes: !! THE TWO-SIDED REQUIREMENT IS THE DESIGN CONTENT, not the position. At the STANDARD 600 mm depth two back-to-back carcasses are 1200 mm before any structure between them - see ENV-WARDROBE-DEEP, corrected from 550 on 2026-09-18. Sequenced LAST: it depends on the hall/kids boundary and the children's bed positions, and starting here would let a joinery idea dictate the zoning by accident.

statement: Room ROLES are deliberately unfixed - see occupancy_scenarios.csv. The girl stays in the middle room in both Phase-2 scenarios.
notes: !! REPLACED BY THE SCENARIO TABLE on 2026-09-18. This row used to record a single role swap as settled. The owner: «I want to change the layout, change the place - who will be living where, where exactly - EASILY.» A single assignment was the wrong shape for that; what is stable is the FAMILY and their daily scenarios, not which room each person is in.

statement: A transformable bedroom zone inside the kitchen/living area, separated by a FULLY RETRACTABLE GLASS partition of four or five folding leaves.
notes: !! THE GOVERNING INTENT, AND ITS PURPOSE IS NOT TO PICK A LAYOUT. Both Phase-2 scenarios in occupancy_scenarios.csv use this same zone and differ only in WHO sleeps there - adults in SC-A, the boy in SC-B. !! SO THE DESIGN QUESTION IS: what first-fix serves BOTH? The owner's own reasoning: «we won't be able to change the engineering systems - electric wiring, lighting, some of the furniture - so I would like to model both possible placements.» Wiring, lighting and ventilation are decided once, at rough stage, and everything else can move later.

statement: No bunk beds in the kids' room.
notes: A household preference, and it costs nothing - the vault's own sources argue against bunks where area permits two separate beds, and it does.

statement: CONSTANT: the family - two adults, two children - their requirements, way of life and daily scenarios; and the reinforced-concrete columns and frame. VARIABLE: everything else, including the room dividers.
notes: !! THIS IS THE PROJECT'S OWN STRUCTURAL/INFILL SPLIT, STATED BY THE OWNER, and it matches what the model already enforces: `concrete` walls are structural and no variant may move them. !! THE DIVIDERS ARE EXPLICITLY IN PLAY: «even the room dividers... most likely we're not going to destroy them completely, probably move just a little bit - the small dividers.» He estimated those at 35 mm; the model records G6, G7 and G8 at 75 mm, which is the figure to use until someone measures one. Either way they are thin infill and moving them is cheap - which is exactly why the EXPENSIVE decisions are the wiring and lighting, not the walls.

statement: DAYLIGHT IS ALLOCATED TO STUDY POSITIONS FIRST. The window wall takes the desk; beds go deeper into the room, away from the window.
anchored_to: every room with a window - today the shared children's room at O2
notes: Owner: «windows are important for studying - to place a table with good lighting, which is very important for kids, especially pupils.» !! IT IS A RULE ABOUT WHAT DAYLIGHT IS SPENT ON, not about furniture, and that is why it generalises: any room with a window inherits it, and it will decide desk positions in BOTH Phase-2 scenarios and in the shared room today. !! ITS FIRST CONSEQUENCE IS A REFUSAL, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES IT REAL. R8 and R9 offer 1490 mm concrete spans that would take a wall bed, and the owner rejects them because they flank the window wall MB carrying O2. A structurally valid position refused on daylight grounds is a design decision the geometry could never have produced. ⚠️ AND IT HAS A FIRST-FIX CONSEQUENCE, which is the whole reason DI-004 is sequenced first: a desk at the window needs sockets and task lighting AT the window, and a bed deep in the room needs its own. Both must be in the rough wiring, because neither moves cheaply afterwards.

statement: EVERY ROOM IS BANDED ALONG ITS ENTRANCE-TO-WINDOW AXIS, in this order: (1) entrance band - built-in wardrobe / storage; (2) middle band - the bed; (3) window band - table, study or seating.
anchored_to: every room; the kitchen/living zone takes a modified form
notes: Owner: «when we enter the room we have a wardrobe, built-in wardrobe; then we have a bed; then we have the area near the window... this is kind of a universal rule as I see it now.» !!⚠️ IT IS AUTHORED, NOT DERIVED, AND A PAGE OF MINE CLAIMED OTHERWISE. Single-sided daylight proves every room shares a depth axis and a light gradient - it does NOT assign storage, bed and study to successive bands. That assignment is the owner's design decision. THE COUNTEREXAMPLE IS ALREADY CANONICAL: PAR-KIDS-BED-PLACEMENT puts beds beside R4/R5, at the entrance end, which is the band this rule gives to storage. A derived rule could not contradict itself that way; an authored one can. What the geometry DOES contribute is that the rule is CHECKABLE - one depth axis means a placement can be tested against the ordering. That is a property of the rule's shape, not evidence for its content. !! THE KITCHEN/LIVING ZONE TAKES A MODIFIED FORM: the KITCHEN is an extra band BEYOND the storage one - «the farthest from the window, it has less light» - and the living part has no distinct wardrobe band, «probably we can replace it with some storage placements». ⚠️ AND THERE IS AN UNRESOLVED TENSION IN THE LIVING ZONE - see BAND-KL-3. The owner does not think there is room for a table at that window, so the bed shifts toward it; but in SC-B the BOY occupies that zone and needs a table. Both cannot hold at once, and which gives way is NOT decided.
